Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
Structured code review stands among the most effective practices an engineering team can adopt to improve software quality, and its benefits manifest across technical, organizational, and long-term dimensions of software development.

The most immediate and measurable benefit of code review lies in defect detection. When a second engineer examines a change before it is merged, they bring fresh eyes to logic that the author may have grown too close to see clearly. Edge cases that went unconsidered, null pointer risks buried in conditional branches, race conditions in concurrent code, and incorrect assumptions about input data are routinely surfaced during review. The economic argument here is compelling and well established: a bug caught during review costs minutes of a reviewer's time to flag and perhaps an hour of the author's time to fix, whereas the same bug discovered after release can cascade into customer support tickets, emergency patches, data corruption cleanup, lost revenue, and reputational damage. Studies of defect economics have consistently shown that the cost of fixing a bug grows by roughly an order of magnitude as it moves from development to testing to staging to production, which makes the pre-merge review window one of the highest-leverage moments in the entire software lifecycle.

Beyond catching defects, code review serves as a continuous knowledge-sharing mechanism that strengthens the collective capability of the team. When engineers review each other's changes, they are necessarily exposed to parts of the system they might otherwise never touch. Over time, this exposure builds a shared mental model of the codebase, so that no single engineer becomes the sole person who understands the authentication layer, the billing pipeline, or the data ingestion service. This diffusion of knowledge directly reduces the operational risk that comes from relying on individual experts, whether that risk manifests as blocked work during vacations, panic during on-call incidents, or crises when a key engineer leaves the company. Review also tends to be a vehicle for mentorship in both directions, as senior engineers model good practices for juniors and juniors raise questions that prompt seniors to articulate and sometimes reconsider their reasoning. The result is a team whose depth of expertise expands rather than concentrating in a few irreplaceable individuals.

Finally, the regular practice of review enforces consistent coding standards in a way that no automated linter or style guide can fully accomplish on its own. Reviewers naturally push back on inconsistent naming, unclear abstractions, duplicated logic, poorly structured tests, and departures from established architectural patterns, and over time this steady pressure converges the codebase toward a coherent style. Consistency in a codebase is not a cosmetic concern; it is a direct multiplier of maintainability, because engineers can navigate familiar structures quickly, predict where functionality lives, and modify code with confidence that similar changes have been handled in similar ways elsewhere. A codebase shaped by sustained review reads as the work of a single thoughtful author rather than a chaotic collage, and this quality pays dividends every time the software must be extended, debugged, or handed to a new contributor. Taken together, the defect prevention, knowledge distribution, and standards enforcement that structured review provides make it one of the most durable investments an engineering team can make in the quality of what it builds.

--- RESPONSE B ---
Structured code review acts as a critical quality assurance gate that intercepts bugs, logical errors, and security vulnerabilities before they ever reach the production environment. When a peer examines code with a fresh set of eyes, they can identify edge cases and flaws that the original author, who is often too close to the implementation, might have easily overlooked. Catching these defects during the development phase is exponentially cheaper and less disruptive than resolving them after release. In production, a bug can lead to system downtime, compromised user data, and lost revenue, requiring emergency hotfixes, patches, and extensive regression testing. By resolving these issues during the review stage, engineering teams save valuable time, protect the organization's reputation, and maintain a stable, reliable product for their users.

Beyond immediate bug detection, structured code review serves as a powerful mechanism for knowledge sharing and team resilience. When engineers regularly examine one another's code, they gain exposure to different parts of the system, learning about architectural patterns, third-party integrations, and business logic they might not interact with directly in their daily tasks. This collective familiarity dismantles information silos and significantly mitigates the risk associated with relying on a single expert for critical components of the application. If a key developer leaves the team or is temporarily unavailable, other team members can confidently step in to debug, update, or expand that area of the codebase because they have already engaged with it during the review process, ensuring business continuity.

Finally, the practice of regular peer review is essential for establishing and enforcing consistent coding standards across the entire engineering organization. Without a collaborative review process, individual developers tend to write code in their own unique styles, leading to a fragmented and disjointed codebase that becomes increasingly difficult to read and understand. Structured reviews ensure that every contribution adheres to agreed-upon formatting, naming conventions, and architectural guidelines. This consistency makes the software far easier to maintain over time, as any engineer can open a file and immediately understand its structure and intent without having to decipher a colleague's idiosyncratic style. Ultimately, this uniform codebase accelerates future development velocity, simplifies onboarding for new team members, and lowers the long-term cost of software ownership.

--- RESPONSE C ---
Structured code review serves as a vital practice that enhances the overall quality of software developed by engineering teams. By having peers examine proposed changes before they are integrated into the main codebase, teams are able to identify and resolve defects at an early stage, which proves significantly less expensive than addressing issues that surface only after the software has been deployed to production environments where fixes often require extensive testing, coordination, and potential downtime. 

The collaborative examination of modifications also promotes a broader understanding of the entire codebase among team members, thereby diminishing the dependency on individual experts who might otherwise become bottlenecks during development or maintenance tasks. 

In addition, the consistent application of review standards ensures that all code adheres to established conventions and practices, resulting in software that is more straightforward to maintain and evolve over extended periods as new features are added or existing ones are updated.

--- RESPONSE D ---
Structured code review significantly enhances the quality of software by identifying defects early in the development process, fostering team-wide knowledge sharing, and ensuring consistent coding practices. One of the most immediate benefits of code review is the ability to catch defects before they reach production. Bugs discovered during the development phase are far less costly to address than those found after release, where they can lead to customer dissatisfaction, downtime, and expensive hotfixes. By systematically examining each change, reviewers can spot logical errors, edge cases, and potential vulnerabilities that might have been overlooked by the original author. This proactive approach not only reduces the risk of critical failures but also contributes to a more stable and reliable end product.

Beyond defect detection, code review plays a crucial role in spreading knowledge across the engineering team. When developers review each other’s work, they gain exposure to different parts of the codebase and learn from the approaches and techniques employed by their peers. This shared understanding reduces the team’s reliance on individual experts, who might otherwise become bottlenecks or single points of failure. Over time, this collective familiarity with the codebase empowers more team members to contribute confidently to various areas of the project, enhancing overall productivity and resilience. It also fosters collaboration and mentorship, as less experienced developers can learn from the insights of their more seasoned colleagues.

Finally, structured code review enforces consistent coding standards, which are essential for maintaining software over its lifecycle. When reviewers assess code for readability, style, and adherence to best practices, they ensure that the codebase remains clean, uniform, and easy to understand. This consistency simplifies debugging, refactoring, and extending the software, as developers can quickly navigate and modify code without encountering inconsistencies or confusing patterns. By embedding these standards into the review process, teams create a culture of quality that persists across individual contributions, ultimately resulting in software that is not only functional but also sustainable and scalable over time.

--- RESPONSE E ---
Structured code review improves software quality by giving teams a disciplined opportunity to catch defects before code reaches users. Reviewers can identify logic errors, missing edge-case handling, incorrect assumptions, security weaknesses, performance issues, and inadequate tests while the change is still fresh and inexpensive to correct. At that stage, the developer still has the context in mind, the affected code is isolated, and the fix usually requires only a small adjustment. Once the same defect reaches production, it can trigger customer impact, urgent incident response, data repair, hotfix coordination, and loss of trust, all of which make the cost far higher. By moving defect discovery earlier in the development process, structured review directly raises the quality of released software.

Reviewing each other’s changes also spreads knowledge of the codebase across the team. Every review exposes engineers to modules, patterns, business rules, dependencies, and design decisions they might not encounter in their own feature work. Over time, this shared visibility reduces reliance on single experts who are the only people familiar with a critical area. More engineers become capable of diagnosing problems, extending features, and making informed architectural decisions. That broader ownership makes the team more resilient and helps ensure that quality does not depend on one person’s availability or memory.

Regular review further improves quality by enforcing consistent coding standards. When teams repeatedly examine changes against shared expectations for naming, structure, testing, error handling, documentation, and design style, those expectations become part of everyday engineering practice. Consistency makes the software easier to read, reason about, modify, and debug because engineers do not have to relearn conventions from file to file or component to component. As the codebase grows, this maintainability becomes a major quality advantage: future changes can be made with greater confidence, lower risk, and less accidental complexity.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
Now output the JSON object described above, and nothing else.
